claims.text: Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength despite favorable plasticity.
The low hardness and strength of this CoCrFeNiTi state arise from unusually high dislocation mobility and pronounced dynamic recovery.
Rapid dislocation annihilation and rearrangement limit the buildup of strain-hardening dislocation networks.
The applicable starting material is single-phase equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with low pre-existing dislocation density.
Dislocation nucleation, mobility, cross-slip, and recovery govern the evolution of work hardening during deformation.
The simple solid solution has low lattice friction.
Low lattice friction makes dislocations easy to generate and highly mobile in CoCrFeNiTi.
Moderate-to-low strain rates or slightly elevated temperatures permit rapid dislocation rearrangement and annihilation.
Dynamic recovery prevents significant strain hardening and thereby produces high plasticity together with low hardness and strength.
High strain rates or lower temperatures should restrict recovery and produce a modest increase in dislocation density.
The recovery-restricting conditions should increase measured hardness and strength relative to the starting or moderate-rate state.
Low strain rates or slightly elevated temperatures should yield less dislocation-density buildup and persistently lower hardness and strength.
Moderate-rate room-temperature tests provide a baseline exhibiting low hardness and strength together with high plasticity due to dynamic recovery.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase CoCrFeNiTi under uniaxial tension or compression at ambient or near-ambient temperatures without precipitation or phase transformation.
Invariant dislocation density, arrangement, and work hardening across strain-rate and temperature changes would falsify dynamic recovery as the governing mechanism.
